title: The diamond sent away
hook: the Koh-i-Noor is taken from the boy king and sent to Queen Victoria

segments.voice: Yesterday, bandhan, and your line was the kingdom ended. Today, a stone that stood for that kingdom leaves it.

A small box, and inside it a single great diamond. Ranjit Singh wore it on his arm at court. Afghan rulers held it before him, and Mughal emperors before them. Its name, the Koh-i-Noor, is usually given in English as the mountain of light. When the Punjab was annexed, the terms said this stone would go to the Queen of England. It was taken from a boy who was still a child.
screen: `A STONE IN A SMALL BOX.` → `WORN ON A MAHARAJA'S ARM.` → `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Koh-i-Noor had passed from ruler to ruler, often by force. Ranjit Singh obtained it from an Afghan king, Shah Shuja, who had come to him as a refugee, and the circumstances are still argued over. At Lahore it became a sign of the kingdom itself. When Lord Dalhousie annexed the Punjab, the agreement named the Koh-i-Noor and said it was to be surrendered to the Queen. Dalhousie wanted it sent as a prize of the war, not as a gift from the Maharaja. A story is told in the life of John Lawrence, one of the officers then governing the Punjab: the stone was handed to him in its little box, he slipped it into a pocket and forgot it, and when he was asked for it he had a bad moment searching. Then it went under guard to the coast and by ship to Britain. There it was cut down to a new shape and became part of the crown jewels. Its return has been asked for, from more than one country, and the question is still open. In Sikh tellings, the diamond isn't really about wealth. It's about a child who lost his kingdom and then lost its sign too. Guru Nanak, in a hymn tradition links to the invasion of Babur, says that for the sake of wealth many were ruined and disgraced; it can't be gathered without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go with you when you die.
screen: `A STONE THAT PASSED FROM HAND TO HAND.` · `NAMED IN THE TERMS.` · `A BOX IN A POCKET, THEN A SHIP.` · `WHAT WEALTH CANNOT CARRY.` · then, large: `TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands palm up on your knees and bring to mind one thing you hold onto tightly: an object, a role, a picture of how things should be. On each breath out, let the fingers soften a little; you aren't giving anything away, only noticing that your hands can be open while the thing is still yours. If you pray, say Waheguru softly as they open.
Moh, attachment, the grip that won't open, the Gurus warn: the Koh-i-Noor, worn by Ranjit Singh, taken from his son for the Queen. Today's word.
Your line: taken away. The box held more than a stone. Day nine hundred forty.
